tips.title: The angle is to the shadow
tips.body: The angle between a **line and a plane** is the angle between the line and its **shadow** on that plane. For a space diagonal and the base, the shadow is the **base diagonal** — so that is always the first thing to find.

tips.title: Use tan, because you already have both sides
tips.body: $\tan \theta = \dfrac{\text{height}}{\text{base diagonal}}$ needs only the two sides you find first. Sin and cos also need the space diagonal, which is extra work and an extra chance to slip — though computing one of them afterwards is a free check.

tips.title: Compare the height with the base diagonal first
tips.body: Height **longer** than the base diagonal means the angle is **more** than 45°; shorter means less; equal means exactly 45°. Knowing roughly what to expect catches the classic error of swapping opposite and adjacent, which returns $90 - \theta$.

tips.title: Never round the base diagonal
tips.body: Carry it in the calculator rather than writing down a rounded value and typing it back. For a 2 by 3 base, rounding $\sqrt{13}$ to 3.6 moves the angle by about 0.1°, which is enough to fall outside the accepted range.

why.matters:
In two dimensions an angle is between two lines. In three, the angle that usually matters is between a **line and a flat surface** — a cable and the ground, a diagonal and the floor.

The method never changes: find the right-angled triangle that contains the angle, which means dropping the line onto the surface and joining it up. What makes it hard is seeing that triangle inside a solid, and what makes it worth the effort is that the answer is rarely the angle you would have guessed.

examples.title: The rafter that is not cut at the roof pitch
examples.body:
A roof has a pitch of 40°. Every common rafter runs straight up the slope at that angle, and a carpenter cuts them all the same.

Then there is the hip: the rafter along the corner, where two slopes meet. It rises to the same ridge, so it seems as though it should be cut at 40° too. It must not be. It travels across the **diagonal** of the corner, which is $\sqrt{2}$ times as far for the same rise, so its angle is shallower — 30.7°.

That is 9.3° out. A hip rafter cut at 40° does not sit down on the wall plate and the timber is scrap, which is why every carpenter's reference has a hip table in it.

The geometry is exactly the syllabus: the angle between a line and a plane, found by dropping the hip onto the horizontal and using the right-angled triangle that appears.

steps.title: The angle between a line and a plane
steps.body:
This topic is **Higher tier**, and it builds directly on 3D Pythagoras.

A typical question asks for the **angle between the space diagonal and the base** of a cuboid. That phrase — *the angle between a line and a plane* — has a precise meaning, and understanding it is most of the work.

Imagine the space diagonal running from a bottom corner up to the opposite top corner. Now shine a light straight down: the diagonal casts a **shadow** on the base. That shadow is the **base diagonal**.

The angle you want is the angle between the line and its own shadow.

So the triangle you need has:

- the **base diagonal** lying flat (the shadow);
- the **vertical edge** going straight up;
- the **space diagonal** as the hypotenuse.

It is the same upright triangle as in 3D Pythagoras. The difference is that now you want the **angle** rather than the third side — and since you can always find the base diagonal, you always have two sides, which is enough.

steps.title: Finding the angle
steps.body:
The method is three steps, and the first is always the same.

1. Find the **base diagonal** with 2D Pythagoras.
2. Draw the upright triangle, flat and separately.
3. Use **tan**, because you have the opposite and the adjacent.

steps.title: All three ratios agree
steps.body:
Once you have found the base diagonal, you actually know **all three** sides of the upright triangle: base $5$, height $12$, hypotenuse $13$. So any of the three ratios will give the same angle.

- $\tan \theta = \dfrac{12}{5}$ gives $67.38°$
- $\sin \theta = \dfrac{12}{13}$ gives $67.38°$
- $\cos \theta = \dfrac{5}{13}$ gives $67.38°$

Use **tan** by preference, for one reason: it needs only the two sides you find **first**, the base diagonal and the vertical edge. Using sin or cos means finding the space diagonal as well, which is extra work and an extra chance to slip.

But knowing that all three agree gives you a free **check**. If you have time, compute the angle a second way. If the two disagree, one of your sides is wrong.

**A caution about rounding.** Use the **unrounded** base diagonal in the ratio. Rounding $\sqrt{13}$ to $3.6$ before dividing can shift the angle by a few tenths of a degree, which is enough to lose the accuracy mark.

check.prompt: A cuboid measures 6 cm by 8 cm by 10 cm. What is the angle between its space diagonal and the base, in degrees?
check.solution: Base diagonal $= \sqrt{36 + 64} = 10$ cm, equal to the height, so $\tan \theta = 1$ and $\theta = 45°$.

steps.title: Other angles in the same box
steps.body:
Not every question asks for the angle with the base. Read carefully which angle is wanted, because the triangle changes.

- **Space diagonal and the base**: the triangle is base diagonal, height, space diagonal. Use $\tan \theta = \dfrac{\text{height}}{\text{base diagonal}}$.
- **Space diagonal and a vertical edge**: the same triangle, but now the angle is at the **top**, so the roles of opposite and adjacent swap: $\tan \theta = \dfrac{\text{base diagonal}}{\text{height}}$.
- **Face diagonal and an edge**: a flat triangle on one face, no 3D work at all.

The two angles in the upright triangle add to **90°**, since the third angle is the right angle. So if the angle with the base is $67.38°$, the angle with the vertical edge is $90 - 67.38 = 22.62°$. That is a quick way to get the second one, and a good check on the first.

**The habit that prevents most errors**: before calculating, label which side is **opposite** the angle you want and which is **adjacent** to it. In 3D those roles are easy to swap by accident, and swapping them turns $\theta$ into $90 - \theta$.

steps.title: Going deeper: reading the question, and running it backwards
steps.body:
**Reading which angle is wanted.** The commonest lost mark here is not arithmetic but comprehension. *The angle between AG and the base* is not the same as *the angle between AG and the edge AE*. Before calculating, write down which two things the angle is between, and which triangle contains both. Thirty seconds there saves the whole question.

A reliable test: the angle between a line and a **plane** is always measured to the line's **shadow** on that plane. If the question names a plane, find the shadow.

**Running it backwards.** A question may give the angle and ask for a length.

> A cuboid has a base 4 cm by 3 cm. What height gives an angle of 45° with the base?

The base diagonal is 5 cm. For 45°, $\tan 45° = 1$, so

$$\frac{\text{height}}{5} = 1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \text{height} = 5 \text{ cm}$$

The height must equal the base diagonal. That is the general rule behind the 45° case, and it is worth stating as a sentence rather than a number.

**Accuracy.** Keep the base diagonal unrounded. For a 2 by 3 base the diagonal is $\sqrt{13} = 3.6055\ldots$; rounding to 3.6 before dividing shifts the angle by about 0.1°, which is enough to fall outside the accepted range. Store it in your calculator rather than writing it down and typing it back in.

**A sense check that always works.** If the vertical edge is **longer** than the base diagonal, the angle is **more** than 45°; if it is shorter, **less**. Compare the two numbers before you calculate, and you will know roughly what to expect. An answer of 22° where you expected 67° usually means opposite and adjacent were swapped — which is exactly the error that turns $\theta$ into $90 - \theta$.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- This topic is **Higher tier**; the Foundation specification stops at two-dimensional figures.
- The angle between a **line and a plane** is the angle between the line and its **shadow** on that plane.
- For a space diagonal and the base, the shadow is the **base diagonal**.
- **Method**: find the base diagonal, draw the upright triangle flat, then use **tan**.
- $\tan \theta = \dfrac{\text{height}}{\text{base diagonal}}$.
- For a 4 by 3 by 12 cuboid: base diagonal $5$ cm, $\tan \theta = \dfrac{12}{5}$, $\theta = 67.4°$.
- **All three ratios agree** once you know all three sides, which gives you a free check.
- Prefer **tan**, because it uses the two sides you find first.
- The angle with the **vertical edge** is $90°$ minus the angle with the base.
- **Keep the base diagonal unrounded** in the ratio. Rounding it can shift the angle enough to lose the mark.
- **Sense check**: height longer than the base diagonal means more than 45°, shorter means less.
- The angle is exactly **45°** when the height **equals** the base diagonal.
- Read carefully which angle is wanted. Swapping opposite and adjacent turns $\theta$ into $90 - \theta$.

questions.prompt: A cuboid measures 5 cm by 12 cm by 7 cm. Find the angle between its space diagonal and the base, showing your method, and check your answer using a different trigonometric ratio.
questions.solution: The first step is to find the diagonal of the base, using Pythagoras on the five by twelve rectangle. Five squared plus twelve squared is twenty five plus one hundred and forty four, which is one hundred and sixty nine, and the square root of that is thirteen, so the base diagonal is thirteen centimetres. The triangle needed for the angle has the base diagonal of thirteen centimetres lying flat, the vertical edge of seven centimetres going straight up, and the space diagonal as its hypotenuse. The angle with the base has the vertical edge opposite it and the base diagonal adjacent to it, so the correct ratio is tangent. Tan of the angle is seven divided by thirteen, which is zero point five three eight, and taking the inverse tangent gives twenty eight point three degrees to one decimal place. To check this using a different ratio, first find the space diagonal, which is the square root of one hundred and sixty nine plus forty nine, that is the square root of two hundred and eighteen, or about fourteen point seven six centimetres. Then sine of the angle is seven divided by fourteen point seven six, which gives the same angle of twenty eight point three degrees, confirming the answer.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Step 1: the base diagonal.**

$$\sqrt{5^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{25 + 144} = \sqrt{169} = 13 \text{ cm}$$

**Step 2: the triangle.** Base $13$ cm flat, height $7$ cm upright, space diagonal as hypotenuse.

**Step 3: the ratio.** The vertical edge is **opposite** and the base diagonal **adjacent**, so use **tan**:

$$\tan \theta = \frac{7}{13} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \theta = 28.3°$$

**The check.** Space diagonal $= \sqrt{169 + 49} = \sqrt{218} \approx 14.76$ cm. Then

$$\sin \theta = \frac{7}{14.76} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \theta = 28.3° \ ✓$$

The two agree, so the sides were right. And the sense check holds: the height is **shorter** than the base diagonal, so the angle is **less** than 45°.

questions.prompt: Explain why the angle between the space diagonal and the base of a cuboid is exactly 45° when the cuboid measures 6 cm by 8 cm by 10 cm, and state the general condition for this angle to be 45°.
questions.solution: The base of the cuboid is six centimetres by eight centimetres, so its diagonal is the square root of thirty six plus sixty four, which is the square root of one hundred, or ten centimetres. The triangle used to find the angle has this base diagonal of ten centimetres lying flat and the vertical edge of ten centimetres standing upright. The tangent of the angle is the opposite over the adjacent, which is ten divided by ten, giving exactly one, and the angle whose tangent is one is forty five degrees. In general, the angle between the space diagonal and the base is forty five degrees precisely when the height of the cuboid is equal to the diagonal of its base, because that is what makes the tangent equal to one. It is worth noting that this does not require the cuboid to be a cube, since this example is six by eight by ten and is clearly not one.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The base diagonal.**

$$\sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{36 + 64} = \sqrt{100} = 10 \text{ cm}$$

**Why 45°.** The height is also **10 cm**, so in the upright triangle the opposite and adjacent sides are **equal**:

$$\tan \theta = \frac{10}{10} = 1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \theta = 45°$$

**The general condition.** The angle is exactly 45° **whenever the height equals the diagonal of the base**, because that is what makes the tangent equal to 1.

**A caution.** This does **not** mean the cuboid is a cube. Here it is 6 by 8 by 10, plainly not one — the condition is about the height matching the base *diagonal*, not the base edges.

examTechnique.body:
Write down which two things the angle is between before doing anything else. If it is a line and a plane, find the line's shadow on that plane.

Find the base diagonal first, and keep it in the calculator unrounded.

Sketch the upright triangle separately and label which side is opposite the angle and which is adjacent. In three dimensions these are easy to swap, and swapping them gives $90 - \theta$.

Use tan by preference. If you have time, check with sin or cos, which needs the space diagonal as well.

Sense check before you calculate: compare the height with the base diagonal and decide whether to expect more or less than 45°.

Give angles to 1 decimal place unless told otherwise, and include the degree symbol.
examinerErrors: Measuring the angle to an edge of the base instead of to the base diagonal.
Swapping opposite and adjacent, which returns 90 − θ.
Rounding the base diagonal before dividing.
Using the space diagonal as the adjacent side.
Answering for the angle with the vertical edge when the base was asked for.
Assuming a 45° answer means the shape is a cube.
Omitting the degree symbol or the decimal place asked for.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer identifies the plane and finds the shadow before reaching for a ratio, so it never measures to the wrong line. It labels opposite and adjacent explicitly, which is what prevents the $90 - \theta$ error that no arithmetic check would catch. It predicts whether the angle is above or below 45° by comparing the height with the base diagonal, then confirms with the calculation rather than trusting it blindly. Where time allows it verifies with a second ratio, and it keeps every intermediate value in the calculator so the final rounding is the only one.
